query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy provides a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor integrity and tends to crack. Prior studies on related MM′X materials used epoxy-containing Mn0.98CoGe, obtaining compressive strengths of 152 and 218 MPa at two epoxy contents, and low-melting In composites, obtaining 48 MPa compressive strength and more than eight times the thermal conductivity of epoxy-containing samples under the reported conditions. These routes demonstrated gains in selected strength or heat-transport metrics, but the desired coexistence of robust integrity and high caloric performance remains unresolved. The target should also remain rare-earth-free. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing caloric response? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, quantitative or directional outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, boundary conditions under applied-field, pressure, temperature, and loading regimes, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive controlled experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding 1–2 at.% Nb to (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 will trigger the in situ formation of coherent, nanometric Nb-rich precipitates that enhance the alloy’s mechanical integrity by impeding crack propagation and refining grain boundaries while preserving its large caloric response.
generation.material_initial_state: (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 exhibits strong field‐induced caloric effects but suffers from poor mechanical integrity and crack propagation under compressive loads.
generation.intervention: Introduce a microalloying addition of 1–2 at.% niobium (Nb) to the base alloy.
generation.conditions: The alloy is operated under applied magnetic and pressure fields, at temperatures around its caloric transformation range, and under compressive mechanical loading similar to previous tests.
generation.structural_mediator: In situ formation of coherent, nanometric Nb-rich precipitates localized at the grain boundaries, which act as crack stoppers and refine the microstructure.
generation.mechanism: The Nb-rich precipitates strengthen the matrix by pinning grain boundaries and obstructing crack propagation, thus increasing compressive strength and toughness while the low-volume Nb addition does not significantly alter the phase responsible for the large caloric response.
generation.predicted_outcome: An increase in compressive strength to levels approaching or exceeding 218 MPa, with the caloric entropy change maintained within ±10% of that in the unmodified alloy.
generation.baseline: The unmodified (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy shows high caloric performance but poor mechanical integrity with crack-prone behavior and lower compressive strength.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies under the same thermal, applied-field (magnetic or pressure), and compressive loading conditions as those used in the baseline evaluation of the unmodified alloy.
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainty remains regarding the exact precipitate volume fraction and distribution needed to optimize both mechanical and caloric properties and the potential sensitivity of the caloric response to slight compositional changes.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of the alloy: one with 1–2 at.% Nb added and one control without Nb. Process both batches identically. Use TEM/SEM to verify the presence and distribution of Nb-rich precipitates. Evaluate both batches under identical conditions using compressive strength tests and caloric response measurements (e.g., magnetocaloric or barocaloric cycling) to assess changes in mechanical performance and caloric entropy.
measurements: Microstructural analysis (grain size and precipitate distribution)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if the Nb-doped alloy does not show a statistically significant improvement in compressive strength (i.e. remains below ~218 MPa or shows no reduction in crack propagation) or if its caloric entropy change is reduced by more than 10% compared to the control alloy.

frame.system: (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy in its starting state exhibits a strong caloric transformation but shows brittle behavior with cracking under mechanical load
frame.goal: Achieve robust structural integrity (higher compressive strength and fracture resistance) while maintaining the large field‐induced caloric response, without incorporating rare-earth elements
frame.limitation: The alloy tends to crack and has poor mechanical integrity, and previous composite approaches have only improved selected metrics (either strength or thermal conductivity) rather than delivering a solution that couples robust mechanics with high caloric performance
root_cause_cues: desired coexistence of robust integrity and high caloric performance remains unresolved
constraints: the intervention must be a single modification
must not sacrifice the large caloric response
operational conditions include applied-field and pressure-field regimes
frame.regime: The material operates under applied magnetic/pressure fields, variable temperatures around the caloric transformation range, and under mechanical load (compressive tests as referenced by prior epoxy/In composite tests)
prior_attempts: Epoxy-containing Mn0.98CoGe composites achieved compressive strengths of 152 and 218 MPa at varying epoxy contents, but may compromise thermal pathways and possibly interact with the caloric mechanism

Low-melting In composites improved thermal conductivity markedly (over eight times that of the epoxy system) yet only achieved 48 MPa compressive strength, indicating insufficient mechanical reinforcement
frame.hypothesis: A single intervention that could meet these dual requirements is to introduce a small microalloying addition, such as approximately 1–2 at.% niobium (Nb), into the base (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy. The Nb is expected to promote in situ formation of coherent, nanometric Nb-rich precipitates preferentially along grain boundaries. These precipitates should act as crack stoppers and barriers to dislocation motion, thereby enhancing fracture toughness and compressive strength without significantly altering the matrix composition responsible for the caloric transformation.
frame.mechanism: The Nb-induced precipitates modify the grain boundary structure by providing localized ductility and impeding crack propagation. They also refine the grain size through a pinning effect during processing, resulting in improved mechanical integrity. Because the volume fraction is low, the essential caloric phase transformation is preserved, maintaining the large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field conditions.
frame.expected_outcomes: Quantitatively, one would expect an improvement in compressive strength to a range comparable to or exceeding the upper bound of the epoxy composite cases (i.e., approaching or surpassing 218 MPa) while maintaining the original caloric entropy change (ΔS) within ±10% of the unmodified alloy's performance.
frame.boundary_conditions: The hypothesis applies under the same thermal, magnetic and pressure regimes as the parent alloy (i.e., around the transformation temperature with similar applied fields and under compressive mechanical loading). The intervention must operate without added external phases (only a microalloying addition) and without introducing rare-earth elements.
frame.controlled_experiment: Prepare two sets of (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloys: one set with 1–2 at.% Nb and one control set without Nb. Subject both sets to identical thermo-mechanical processing and characterize their microstructures (using TEM/SEM to confirm the presence and distribution of Nb-rich precipitates). Then, measure their mechanical properties via compressive strength testing and assess caloric performance via field-induced caloric measurements (e.g., magnetocaloric or barocaloric cycling) under identical conditions. A falsification of the hypothesis would be demonstrated if the Nb-modified samples show no significant improvement in mechanical integrity or if the caloric response is reduced by more than approximately 10% relative to the control alloy.

decision.trend: Early research initially attempted to improve the mechanical performance of high‐entropy and medium‐entropy alloys using external composite routes (epoxy or low-melting metal composites) to target either strength or thermal properties, but without addressing the dual need for robust mechanical integrity and preserved caloric response. Later studies shifted toward intrinsic modifications by engineering the microstructure—for instance, through controlled annealing that induces coherent, ordered precipitates (e.g., L12 phases) to strengthen the matrix (as in PMC6478865) and by introducing nanolayer architectures (e.g., graphene interfaces in PMC9227879) that block crack propagation. These approaches successfully enhanced mechanical properties but have yet to be tuned to preserve the significant caloric transformation behavior.
decision.unsolved: The combined challenge of simultaneously achieving enhanced fracture/tensile/compressive strength and maintaining the large field-induced caloric entropy change in a rare-earth-free high-entropy alloy remains unresolved. Prior studies have improved one metric at the expense of other functionalities or relied on multi-phase composites rather than a single alloy system modification.
decision.lever: Introduce a microalloying addition of approximately 1–2 at.% niobium (Nb) into the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy to induce the in situ formation of coherent, nanometric Nb-rich precipitates along grain boundaries.
decision.why: This approach builds on evidence from precipitation-strengthening strategies that yield improved toughness and compressive strength (by blocking crack propagation and refining grains) without significantly altering the matrix phases responsible for the caloric response. It logically extends prior trends that move from external composite reinforcements to subtle intrinsic microstructural modifications, offering a single, composition-based intervention compatible with applied-field, pressure, temperature, and loading regimes.
